messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 55
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Fashion Designer
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 41

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me, Avoid Dreams: Situations or times of day that tend to bring on nightmares, Self-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what I have done wrong
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home
  Memory: No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself, Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
  Negative Appraisals: Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Mistrust: People can't be trusted, Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

David is a fifty-five-year-old fashion designer who walks into the office with the guarded posture of a man accustomed to reading a room for exits. By most external measures, his career has been a success; his collections are known for their architectural precision and clean lines. But that precision, he would confess, is not merely a professional signature. It is a fortress. And inside that fortress, he has been living for decades with the fragments of a childhood he cannot quite narrate to himself.

His father was a man of terrible, watchful silences. The quiet that came before an explosion of rage was, for David, the most dangerous part of the entire ordeal. He learned to read it the way a ground animal reads the shadow of a hawk: a held breath, a tightening in the air that meant something dangerous was about to happen. The physical violence itself—the belt, the back of the hand, the shove into the corner of his bedroom—these moments he can recall with a strange and disturbing numbness, as if they happened to a stranger, a boy he barely recognizes. He can recount the facts without feeling, a cold and disjointed list. But other times, without warning, the numbness shatters and the memory is suffused with an intense, immobilizing guilt. He will find himself obsessively turning over his own childhood actions, dwelling on what he might have done wrong, the misstep that triggered the catastrophe. What did he say? What did he fail to anticipate? Even now, he spends considerable mental energy dwelling bitterly on what his father did to him, but it is the self-blame that feels more insidious, more intimate, a loop he cannot escape.

This internal landscape has shaped his adult life into a series of careful fortifications. He is certain that he has permanently changed for the worse, that the boy he might have been was destroyed long ago and replaced by this vigilant, armored man. The notion that people can be trusted feels to him like a dangerous and naive fantasy. His divorce five years ago was not a single explosive fight but a slow corrosion. His wife grew weary of the distance. What frightened her most, and what he could never adequately explain, was the way he would react with a sharp, visible alarm when she touched him unexpectedly—a flinch, a full-body recoil that felt insulting but was purely autonomic, a survival reflex that had never learned to switch off. She mistook his caution for coldness. He mistook her frustration for proof that he was, indeed, beyond reach.

In his professional life, the strategies he developed to cope have begun to falter. The fashion world demands close physical collaboration. Fittings and draping sessions require assistants to touch him, to adjust a sleeve at the shoulder, to pin a hem at the ankle. His new assistant, a well-meaning young woman, has a habit of approaching from the side, her fingers brushing his arm without warning. Every time, he reacts with the same sharp alarm, his entire body tensing. He has started rearranging his studio so that his back is always to a wall, and he avoids the vulnerable silence of the workshop in the late afternoon, that transitional hush before the evening rush. That particular quiet primes him for the nightmares he dreads, so he pushes himself to work until total exhaustion forces him into unconsciousness. He feels perpetually on guard, even inside his own home, which was supposed to be his refuge but has become just another room to scan for threats.

What finally drove David to reach out for help was a moment of profound terror that occurred in that very home. He was standing alone in his kitchen during an unusual silence—the refrigerator hum had kicked off, the traffic outside had paused—and a wave of sheer panic seized him for no visible reason. He felt the old familiar dread, the held breath from childhood, and he realized he could not tell the difference anymore between a genuine threat and the echoes of a past threat. He looked at his trembling hands and was struck by the horrifying conviction that his reactions meant he was going crazy, that his mind was finally giving way under the weight of the vigilance. He is terrified walking in here that a therapist will confirm his deepest fear: that the damage is permanent and there is nothing left to salvage. Yet beneath that fear, a small and carefully guarded hope persists—that maybe the guilt and the rage and the startle are not the sum total of who he is, but the shape of a wound he can finally learn to touch without being destroyed by it.
